Convex bodies

The Affine Plank Conjecture is about planks covering convex bodies.

A convex body is a shape with no inward curves, like the one shown in red on the leftbelow.

to make it convex.

Planks and relative width

A plank is a region between two parallel lines (or two parallel hyperplanes in higher dimensions).

A plank's relative width is its width divided by the width of the convex body, measured perpendicular to the plank.

The Affine Plank Conjecture

In 1951 Thøger Bang conjectured that if planks cover a convex body, their relative widths must sum to at least 100%.

But nobody has been able to prove this for 75 years.

1 parameter

x position · w relative width · θ angle

Each gap chooses one side of each plank: 2 × 2 × 2 possibilities. Empty cells have area zero.

Gap cells

We call the uncovered regions gap cells.

There are 8 possible gap cells.

The Affine Plank Conjecture is equivalent to saying that when the relative widths of the planks sum to less than one, there is always a gap cell with positive area.

gi(x1, w1, θ1, x2, w2, θ2, x3, w3, θ3) is the area of gap i.

    Full explicit formula

    F and every symbol it uses are defined below.

    s0=1,s1=−1

    2. Triangle boundaries

    The vertices v1, v2, v3 run counterclockwise. Set v4 = v1. Its three outward boundary triples are:

    αr=vr+1,y−vr,y,βr=vr,x−vr+1,x
    Tr=(αr,βr,αrvr,x+βrvr,y)

    3. Shared area formula and all cases

    For F(P1, P2, P3), take the six triples in the order (T1, T2, T3, P1, P2, P3). Write the rth triple as (ar, br, cr).

    F(P1,P2,P3)=∑r=16crer2|K|

    The shared expressions below give er. Both r and s range from 1 to 6.

    Qr=ar2+br2
    Drs=arbs−asbr
    Brs=cs−cr(aras+brbs)Qr

    Each of the other inequalities puts a lower or upper bound on the part of line r that can remain. Take the strongest bounds:

    tr−=maxs:Drs<0BrsDrs
    tr+=mins:Drs>0BrsDrs

    Both sets have a member because the triangle is bounded. Let Xr mean a parallel inequality excludes line r, and Rr mean an earlier line repeats the same outward boundary:

    Xr⇔∃s:Drs=0∧Brs<0
    Rr⇔∃s<r:(Drs=0∧Brs=0∧aras+brbs>0)

    The complete piecewise rule is:

    er={0if Xr∨Rrmax(0,tr+−tr−)otherwise

    Rr counts coincident outward boundaries only once. Opposite boundaries are retained: if the gap collapses to a line, their area contributions cancel.

    This uses only arithmetic, trigonometric functions, finite minima and maxima, and the written conditions. With angles fixed, it is piecewise quadratic in positions and widths.

    Why this gives the area

    Parameterize boundary r by:

    zr(t)=crQr(ar,br)+t(−br,ar)

    Substitution in inequality s gives Drst ≤ Brs, which explains the bounds. A surviving edge runs from tr− to tr+. Its oriented shoelace contribution is crer. Summing the edges, dividing by 2, and dividing by |K| gives the area fraction. An empty intersection has no surviving edges; a point or line has zero area.

    Ers,tu=UrsVtu−VrsUtu

    |K| is the triangle's area. The coefficients depend on the angles; with angles fixed, each piece is quadratic in positions and widths.

    Solving the equations

    So all that remained was to set the area of every gap cell equal to zero and solve.

    As a computer scientist, I thought: finding an intersection of sets is easy.

    For finite sets, yes, but not so for sets of real numbers.

    For polynomial inequalities, a standard general method is cylindrical algebraic decomposition (CAD)…

    But its worst-case running time is doubly exponential in the number of variables, so the naive approach is not feasible, even on the triangle.
